prompt:
# Write one behaviour-tree node that ADJUSTS an existing navigator

You are writing a single node for the behaviour tree of a Unitree Go2 quadruped
navigating an indoor space it has no map of.

Below the node is an inherited, pretrained, **frozen** locomotion policy. The
only thing anything ever sends the robot is a Twist — `(vx, vy, wz)`. You never
touch the policy, the gait, or the joints.

**You are not writing the navigator.** A navigator already exists, it already
drives, and it will keep driving whether or not your node does anything. Your
node sits above it and revises what it asked for.

Return **one Python module**, in one fenced ```python block, and nothing else
that looks like code. Everything you want to say in prose, say outside the
fence. What the module must contain is set out in "What to return" at the end.

## How the tree runs: a layered command pipeline

Every node in the tree ticks, **every step, in order**. Nothing short-circuits
anything.

    Layer[ ports, BASE, node_1, node_2, ... ]
             ^      ^      ^
             |      |      `- each may revise the fields it declared
             |      `-------- proposes a whole command, every tick
             `--------------- publishes a few facts from the sensors

The **base** is a general indoor navigator. It gets the robot most of the way
most of the time, it handles the awkward cases, and it never declines to act.
Each later node may then adjust individual fields of what the base proposed.

This is subsumption: a competent low layer, refined by narrow higher ones. Your
node is one of the higher ones.

**So the thing you are writing is small.** It does one thing to one part of the
command, under one condition, and the rest of the time it stays out of the way.

## The one hard rule: you declare which fields you may write

Your class declares `WRITES` — the Twist fields it is allowed to touch:

```python
WRITES = ("vx",)            # may bound or set forward speed, nothing else
WRITES = ("wz",)            # may steer, but may not change speed
WRITES = ("vx", "wz")       # both. Only if the mechanism genuinely needs both.
```

This is **enforced, not advisory.** Writing a field you did not declare raises
immediately and the node is rejected. Declare the smallest set your mechanism
actually needs — a node that declares all three is claiming to be a navigator,
and it will be judged as one.

Two ways to write, and they are the only two:

```python
ports.cap(vx=0.35)       # min(|pending|, 0.35), sign kept. Never speeds up.
ports.adjust(wz=0.8)     # replaces the field outright. Last writer wins.
```

Prefer `cap` whenever the mechanism is a limit, a bound, or a "no faster than"
— it composes with other caps in any order, which `adjust` does not.

And you can see what the base asked for:

```python
pending = ports.command          # a Command(vx, vy, wz). Never None when you
                                 # tick, because the base ticks before you.
if pending.vx > my_limit:
    ports.cap(vx=my_limit)
```

**Do not call `ports.drive(...)`.** That writes the whole command and is the
base's job; it raises for a node that narrowed `WRITES`.

## Declining is a first-class outcome, and it is free

Return `Status.FAILURE` from `precondition`, or simply write nothing in `tick`,
and the base's command passes through **byte-identical**. The robot behaves
exactly as if your node were not in the tree.

That matters more than it sounds. Your node's contribution is measured by adding
it to the tree and re-running the same worlds: it can only be credited for the
episodes it changes, and it is blamed for every episode it breaks. A node that
acts only when its trigger genuinely holds is a good node. A node that fires on
every tick has replaced the base rather than supported it, and it will be
measured as having done so.

## The node contract

A leaf is one of three kinds, and the kind is the class you subclass:

- **`Condition`** — answers one question about the world and publishes it as a
  port. Never touches the Twist.
- **`Action`** — the only kind that may touch the Twist. With a narrowed
  `WRITES` it is a *modifier*, which is what you are writing.
- **`Decorator`** — wraps exactly one child and governs whether the child runs.
  Never touches the Twist itself.

Your class declares, as class attributes:

| Attribute | What it is |
|---|---|
| `WRITES` | the Twist fields this node may write. See above. |
| `PORTS` | a tuple of `Port` — the typed interface between nodes. See below. |
| `PRECONDITION` | one sentence: when this node applies |
| `EFFECT` | one sentence: what this node changes |
| `TAGS` | a tuple of short strings, for retrieval |

and implements:

```python
def reset(self, scenario, rng):    # clear per-episode state. optional.
def precondition(self, obs, ports) -> bool:   # default: always True
def tick(self, obs, ports) -> Status:         # Status.SUCCESS / FAILURE / RUNNING
```

**One precondition and one effect.** A node that needs two of either is two
nodes. This is not a style rule: contribution is measured by adding one node at
a time, and a node with two effects is attributable to neither.

**No coupling to a specific scenario.** Your node will be run on procedurally
generated worlds you have never seen. It may not name a room, a coordinate, a
doorway or a map. Anything it knows about the world it learns through `obs` at
tick time.

### Ports

Ports are how nodes pass information to each other. They are **not** a
blackboard: at tick time you are handed a `PortView` restricted to exactly the
ports you declared, and touching anything else raises immediately.

```python
Port(name, PortType.X, Direction.IN)    # you read it:   value = ports["name"]
Port(name, PortType.X, Direction.OUT)   # you write it:  ports["name"] = value
```

The port vocabulary is **closed**. These seven types and no others:

| `PortType` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `POSE` | `(x, y, yaw)` — a belief about where the robot is, never ground truth |
| `BEARING` | radians, robot frame unless the port name says otherwise |
| `SPEED` | m/s, non-negative |
| `RANGES` | an array of beam returns, metres |
| `CONFIDENCE` | `[0, 1]` — how much to trust something |
| `FLAG` | a boolean fact about the episode |
| `REGION` | an area of the floor, `(x, y, radius)` |

Three ports are always published before your node ticks, so you may declare any
of them as inputs: `goal_known` (FLAG), `pose` (POSE), `ranges` (RANGES).
Anything else you declare as an input must be published by another node earlier
in the Layer, and if nothing does, the tree refuses to build.

Publish an OUT port when the quantity you computed is genuinely useful to
someone else — a limit, a bearing, a confidence. Do not publish your own
internal state.

### What to import

Exactly these, and nothing else.

```python
import math
import numpy as np

from core.observation import Command
from nodes.contract import (Action, Condition, Decorator, Direction, Port,
                            PortType, Status)
```

Import only what you use. You will usually not need `Command` at all: a modifier
revises fields, it does not construct commands.

### What your node can see

`tick` is handed an `Observation`, frozen, one per control step:

```python
obs.t                   # sim seconds since the episode started
obs.ranges              # np.ndarray, 181 beams, metres, inf where no return
obs.range_angles        # np.ndarray, beam bearings in the ROBOT frame, radians
obs.range_max           # 6.0 — what "as far as I can see" means
obs.pose_estimate       # (x, y, yaw) — the BELIEF about our pose, not the truth
obs.pose_error_estimate # scalar, metres — how wrong we think the belief is
obs.contact             # bool — are we touching something right now
obs.goal                # (x, y), or None meaning NOT DISCLOSED
```

Two of these are traps and both are deliberate:

- **`pose_estimate` is a belief.** On some scenarios a seeded random walk is
  added to it and it drifts away from the truth. Ground truth is never in
  `Observation`; the runner keeps it for scoring only.
- **`obs.goal` may be `None`**, meaning the goal exists and the episode is still
  scored against it, but this robot has not found it yet. It **latches**: once
  disclosed it stays disclosed. Your node runs on scenarios that withhold the
  goal and on scenarios that do not, so **handle `None` explicitly**. Do not
  assume a tuple.

The scan is 181 beams over a full circle, so `obs.ranges[0]` is not the front —
find the beam you want through `obs.range_angles`.

Speeds are saturated by the runner to `|vx|, |vy| <= 0.8 m/s` and
`|wz| <= 1.0 rad/s`. Asking for more is not an error; it is just clipped.

## The task family this node has to be useful for

Reach a goal whose position is known, in an indoor space with no map. Walls and furniture occlude; the route is not a straight line and the obstruction is often not visible until the robot is close to it.

## What to base the node on

A principle card has been written for this task. **Implement this principle and
nothing else.**

```yaml
id: ant_path_integration_goal_vector
node_name: SteerByPathIntegratedGoalVector

mechanism: A Cataglyphis fortis forager continuously maintains a single running estimate of the direction back to its start point, and it does NOT do this by true vector summation (the paper's central negative result). It carries two scalars: phi_n, the mean direction in which it has so far travelled, and l_n, the distance so far travelled counted in unit lengths (strides). Each unit step, having turned by delta relative to phi_n, it rotates its stored direction by an increment that is (a) proportional to a saturating odd function of delta and (b) inversely proportional to l_n. The paper's approximate form is Eq. 2, phi_{n+1} = phi_n + delta / l_n, and the form that fits all their data is Eq. 3:

    phi_{n+1} = phi_n + k * (180deg + delta) * (180deg - delta) * delta / l_n,
    with k = 4.009 x 10^-5 deg^-1

k is exactly the normaliser that makes the numerator peak at 90 degrees (the product is maximal at delta ~= 103.9deg, where it evaluates to 89.99deg), as the paper states. The home direction at any moment is phi_n + 180deg. Why it helps: the 1/l_n term makes the stored direction progressively stiffer the further the animal has walked, so late perturbations - a detour, a stride miscount, a momentary heading wobble - move the home vector by an amount that shrinks as 1/l. It is a one-pole low-pass on bearing whose time constant is distance travelled, and it needs no position variable at all: only turns and step counts. Its price is a known, signed, systematic error (Fig. 2B), largest for near-reversals, and zero at delta = 180deg where the increment vanishes identically. The paper argues this is affordable because left and right turns are equally frequent in nature and their opposite-signed errors cancel (Discussion, p. 5289).

trigger: Fires when the goal has been disclosed (goal is not None) AND at least 1.0 m of commanded translation has accumulated since the integrator's anchor was set, so that l_n >= ~7 unit steps and the 1/l_n damping is actually doing something. Below that threshold the port is false and the tree should fall through to whatever computes goal bearing directly from pose_estimate. The leaf is a bearing source only: it reads no lidar and claims no obstacle competence, so it must sit at lower priority than an avoidance leaf.

derivation: What maps onto what. (i) The ant's drift-free celestial compass maps onto pose_estimate yaw plus the commanded Twist direction. The paper shows the result is unchanged whether the sun or the polarization compass is used (p. 5288), so heading is treated here as the trusted channel and translation as the untrusted one - which is also the split this robot has, since a random walk added to (x, y, yaw) corrupts accumulated displacement far faster than it corrupts instantaneous heading. This split is my reading, not the paper's. (ii) The ant's stride counter (proprioception, not position) maps onto the integral of the Twist this node itself commands: d = sqrt(vx^2 + vy^2) * dt. It deliberately does NOT map onto ||delta pose_estimate||, which would reinject exactly the drift the mechanism is meant to survive. Mine. (iii) The ant's unit length (one stride) maps onto u = 0.15 m. Mine: a Go2 body is ~0.7 m and a comfortable trot stride is roughly a fifth of that, and at the 0.8 m/s speed cap this emits ~5 unit steps per second, which is dense enough for the 1/l_n filter to behave like the continuous Eq. 2 limit the paper takes ("As l_n is much larger than the unit length, Eq. 1a can be transformed (for l -> inf) to Eq. 2"). (iv) The ant integrates toward the nest, i.e. toward the origin of its own path. This robot's goal is a fixed known point that is generally not the path origin, so I extend the scheme: the integrator estimates displacement from an anchor, and the anchor-to-goal offset is carried as a constant. This extension is mine.
State and update, exactly.
  - Anchor: at episode start if goal is not None, else at the first step where
    goal latches from None to known. Store A = (ax, ay) = pose_estimate xy at
    that instant, and the constant offset G = goal - A. Never re-anchor
    afterwards; re-anchoring from a later pose_estimate would import the drift
    accumulated up to that moment. Anchor early: drift is a random walk from
    near zero, so G is least corrupted at the earliest possible anchor.
  - Initialise phi = current world travel direction = wrap(yaw + atan2(vy, vx))
    in degrees (use yaw if commanded speed is zero); l = 1.0 (never let l fall
    below 1.0 - it is the divisor).
  - Each control step accumulate s += sqrt(vx^2 + vy^2) * dt using the Twist
    this node commanded on the previous step. While s >= u = 0.15:
      s -= u
      theta = wrap(yaw + atan2(vy, vx)) in degrees   # direction of this unit step
      delta = wrap_to_(-180, 180](theta - phi)
      dphi  = 4.009e-5 * (180.0 + delta) * (180.0 - delta) * delta / l   # Eq. 3
      dphi  = clip(dphi, -90.0/l, +90.0/l)            # the paper's 90deg cap
      phi   = wrap(phi + dphi)
      l    += 1.0
    Eq. 3 is used verbatim in DEGREES, because k is quoted in deg^-1; convert
    only at the end. Note the built-in behaviour that delta = 180deg gives
    dphi = 0 - a perfect reversal writes nothing into phi. That is the paper's
    own failure mode, not a bug to patch out.
    (The paper also gives a step-length update, Eq. 1b, but that line is not
    legibly reproduced in the text I was given, so I use the unambiguous
    l_{n+1} = l_n + 1 and flag that this differs from the paper if Eq. 1b
    contains a turn-dependent term.)
  - Position estimate, replacing pose_estimate translation entirely:
      p_hat = A + l * u * (cos phi, sin phi)          # phi in radians here
    and the reciprocal home direction phi + 180deg is what the ant would use
    to return to A.
  - Goal bearing: b = wrap_to_(-pi, pi]( atan2(A.y + G.y - p_hat.y,
                                               A.x + G.x - p_hat.x) - yaw ).
  - Output Twist: wz = clip(1.5 * b, -1.0, 1.0) rad/s;
    vx = 0.8 * max(0.0, cos b) m/s; vy = 0.0.
    The gain 1.5 s^-1 is mine, chosen so a 40-degree bearing error saturates
    wz and the turn completes in under a second at the 1.0 rad/s cap.
  - Terminate (SUCCESS) when ||A + G - p_hat|| < 0.5 m; RUNNING otherwise;
    FAILURE if goal is None.
All numbers above except k = 4.009e-5 deg^-1, the 90-degree cap and the 1/l_n and (180+delta)(180-delta)delta structure are mine.

prediction:
  statement: On scenarios where pose_estimate drifts, a robot steering to a goal bearing reconstructed from this Eq.-3 integrator (translation from commanded Twist, heading from yaw, anchored once) reaches the goal on a strictly larger fraction of seeds than the same robot steering to the bearing recomputed each step from pose_estimate directly, because a 1/l_n-damped accumulator fed by proprioception does not inherit the position random walk. It will simultaneously travel further to get there, since Eq. 3 under-rotates phi on near-reversals and near-reversals are common in cluttered indoor space.
  metric: goal_reached
  baseline: goal_seeker
  min_effect: 0.1
  cost_metric: path_length
```

The fields mean what they say, and each one has a job:

- **mechanism** — what happens, and why it helps. This is the node body.
- **trigger** — when it applies. This is the precondition, and under the layered
  pipeline it is doing real work: outside the trigger your node must leave the
  base's command alone.
- **derivation** — how the principle becomes a rule for a Go2 with a 181-beam 2D
  scan. Where the derivation and your instincts disagree, follow the derivation:
  it is what the card is for.
- **prediction** — the falsifiable claim. **Restate it verbatim** in
  `PREDICTION`: the metric, the baseline and the minimum effect are the card's,
  not yours.
- **node_name** — what the leaf is called. Use it as the class name.

You are not told where this principle came from, and you do not need to know.
A card is a card: extracted from a paper, recalled from one, or devised from
nothing, it is implemented the same way and judged by the same harness.

If you believe a different mechanism would score better, that belief is not what
is being measured here — a node that quietly implements something else makes the
card untestable.

**If the principle genuinely cannot be expressed as an adjustment to an existing
navigator, say so in prose and write the closest honest version you can.** Some
mechanisms are whole navigators and this pipeline cannot represent them; that is
a finding about the corpus, and it is more useful than a node that pretends.

## How this node will be judged

Two steps, both automatic, neither of which you can talk round.

1. **Validity.** Your module is loaded, wired into
   `Layer[ports, BASE, your node]`, and ticked over a rollout. It has to build,
   its ports have to be satisfiable, and it must not raise. Writing a Twist
   field you did not declare fails here.
2. **Contribution.** The tree above is run over a suite of randomly generated
   indoor worlds and compared, on identical worlds, against the base alone. What
   is reported is how many worlds your node **fixed** (the base failed, the pair
   succeeded) and how many it **broke** (the reverse).

You do not write the worlds and you have never seen them. There is no
micro-world to build and no baseline to name — that is deliberate, because a
generator that writes both the mechanism and the world that judges it is
grading its own homework.

## Rules the candidate is checked against

Your module is rejected, automatically, if any of these is false. The rejection
is recorded with its reason; it is not a catastrophe, but it is a wasted node.

- It parses, and it imports **only** from this list:
  `math`, `numpy`, `core.observation`, `nodes.contract`, `harness.micro`.
  Nothing else — no `os`, no file access, no `core.scenario`, no `core.geometry`.
  Your node learns about the world through `obs`, and that restriction is what
  makes "no coupling to a specific scenario" true rather than promised.
- It defines **exactly one** `Condition`, `Action` or `Decorator` subclass.
- Every port type is one of the seven. `EFFECT` and `PRECONDITION` are non-empty.
- `WRITES` names only `vx`, `vy` and `wz`, and the node writes nothing outside
  it.

## What to return

One fenced ```python block. It contains exactly two things:

1. **One node class** — normally an `Action` with a narrowed `WRITES`.
2. **`PREDICTION`** — a module-level dict, the card's falsifiable claim:

   ```python
   PREDICTION = {
       "metric": "goal_reached",     # what gets better
       "baseline": "base",           # what it gets better than
       "min_effect": 0.5,            # by at least how much
       "cost_metric": "time_to_goal" # what it makes WORSE. Required, and honest.
   }
   ```

   `cost_metric` may be `""` only if you genuinely believe the mechanism costs
   nothing, and you should be suspicious of that belief.

**No `micro()`.** Do not write one; it is not read.

Put a short docstring on the class saying what mechanism it implements, which
Twist field it revises and why, and when it declines. Write it as you would
write code someone else has to maintain: comments where a choice is not obvious,
and no comments restating the line below them.

response.text:
The card's mechanism is genuinely a *whole* navigator: it specifies both `wz` and `vx` from a bearing it computes itself, and it never consults the lidar. I've implemented it as faithfully as the pipeline allows, with two deliberate deviations I want to flag rather than hide:

- **`vx` is written with `cap`, not `adjust`.** The card asks for `vx = 0.8·max(0, cos b)`, and 0.8 is the runner's own saturation limit — so the expression is a "no faster than while the goal is off the nose" bound, which is exactly what `cap` is for. Capping also means the node cannot undo a slow-down another layer (or the base) already asked for, which `adjust` would.
- **`vy` is left alone.** The card says `vy = 0.0`, but writing it would mean declaring a third field, i.e. claiming to be the navigator. The integrator still *accounts* for whatever `vy` the base commands, since the stride direction is `yaw + atan2(vy, vx)`.

Everything else is verbatim: Eq. 3 in degrees with `k = 4.009e-5 deg⁻¹`, the ±90°/l cap, `l ← l + 1`, `u = 0.15 m`, anchor-once, translation from the commanded Twist rather than from `pose_estimate`, gain 1.5 s⁻¹, 0.5 m arrival.

Two implementation notes. The integrator has to run on *every* tick, including ticks where the node declines — otherwise the 1.0 m trigger never arms — so the bookkeeping lives in `precondition` and `tick` only reads the result. And the distance fed forward is `l·u`, path length, not displacement; that is the mechanism's known systematic error (it over-reads on curved paths, just as Eq. 3 under-rotates on near-reversals), not something to patch out.

```python
import math

from nodes.contract import Action, Direction, Port, PortType, Status

_K = 4.009e-5        # deg^-1, the paper's normaliser: numerator peaks at ~90 deg
_UNIT = 0.15         # m, one "stride" for a Go2 trot
_DPHI_CAP = 90.0     # deg, the paper's ceiling on a single increment (scaled by 1/l)
_TURN_GAIN = 1.5     # s^-1
_CRUISE = 0.8        # m/s
_ARRIVE = 0.5        # m
_ARM_TRAVEL = 1.0    # m of commanded translation before the 1/l damping is meaningful
_MAX_DT = 0.2        # s, guards against a stalled or restarted clock


def _wrap180(a):
    """Wrap degrees to (-180, 180] -- the half-open side matters: delta = 180 must
    survive as +180 so that Eq. 3's (180 - delta) factor zeroes the increment."""
    return 180.0 - ((180.0 - a) % 360.0)


def _wrap_pi(a):
    return math.pi - ((math.pi - a) % (2.0 * math.pi))


class SteerByPathIntegratedGoalVector(Action):
    """Cataglyphis-style path integration (Mueller & Wehner Eq. 3) as a steering source.

    Carries two scalars instead of a position: phi, the mean direction travelled so
    far, and l, distance travelled in unit strides. Each stride it rotates phi by
    k*(180+delta)*(180-delta)*delta/l, so the stored direction stiffens as 1/l and
    late perturbations move the home vector less and less. Displacement from a
    once-set anchor is reconstructed as l*u*(cos phi, sin phi) and the goal bearing
    is taken from that, NOT from pose_estimate -- the whole point is that strides
    come from the commanded Twist (proprioception) while pose_estimate translation
    carries a random walk.

    Revises wz (adjust: steer onto the reconstructed bearing) and vx (cap: no faster
    than 0.8*cos b, so the robot does not cruise while the goal is off the nose).
    It writes neither before the goal has been disclosed, nor before 1.0 m of
    commanded translation has accumulated since the anchor -- below that l is too
    small for the damping to exist and the base's own goal bearing is better. It
    reads no lidar and claims no obstacle competence.
    """

    WRITES = ("vx", "wz")
    PORTS = (
        Port("pi_goal_bearing", PortType.BEARING, Direction.OUT),
        Port("pi_goal_bearing_valid", PortType.FLAG, Direction.OUT),
    )
    PRECONDITION = (
        "The goal has been disclosed and at least 1.0 m of commanded translation "
        "has accumulated since the path integrator was anchored."
    )
    EFFECT = (
        "Drives along the goal bearing reconstructed by the 1/l-damped stride "
        "integrator rather than the bearing implied by the drifting pose estimate."
    )
    TAGS = ("path-integration", "dead-reckoning", "goal-bearing", "drift", "ant")

    # ---------------- state ----------------

    def _clear(self):
        self._anchor = None      # (ax, ay), pose_estimate xy at disclosure time
        self._offset = None      # goal - anchor, frozen at that same instant
        self._phi = 0.0          # deg, mean direction travelled
        self._l = 1.0            # unit steps; never below 1.0, it is the divisor
        self._s = 0.0            # m, sub-stride remainder
        self._travel = 0.0       # m, commanded translation since the anchor
        self._last_t = None
        self._last_cmd = None    # (vx, vy) actually commanded on the previous step
        self._bearing = None

    def _ensure(self):
        if not hasattr(self, "_anchor"):
            self._clear()

    def reset(self, scenario, rng):
        self._clear()

    # ---------------- mechanism ----------------

    def _course_deg(self, yaw, cmd):
        """World-frame direction of travel for a commanded body-frame twist."""
        if cmd is None:
            return math.degrees(_wrap_pi(yaw))
        vx, vy = cmd
        if math.hypot(vx, vy) <= 1e-9:
            return math.degrees(_wrap_pi(yaw))
        return math.degrees(_wrap_pi(yaw + math.atan2(vy, vx)))

    def _try_anchor(self, obs):
        # Anchor at the earliest possible moment: drift is a random walk from near
        # zero, so the anchor-to-goal offset is least corrupted now and must never
        # be recomputed from a later, dirtier pose_estimate.
        if self._anchor is not None or obs.goal is None:
            return
        px, py, yaw = (float(v) for v in obs.pose_estimate)
        self._anchor = (px, py)
        self._offset = (float(obs.goal[0]) - px, float(obs.goal[1]) - py)
        self._phi = self._course_deg(yaw, self._last_cmd)
        self._l = 1.0
        self._s = 0.0
        self._travel = 0.0

    def _integrate(self, yaw, cmd, dt):
        if cmd is None or dt <= 0.0:
            return
        speed = math.hypot(cmd[0], cmd[1])
        if speed <= 0.0:
            return
        course = self._course_deg(yaw, cmd)
        self._s += speed * dt
        self._travel += speed * dt
        while self._s >= _UNIT:
            self._s -= _UNIT
            delta = _wrap180(course - self._phi)
            # Eq. 3 verbatim, in degrees, because k is quoted in deg^-1.
            dphi = _K * (180.0 + delta) * (180.0 - delta) * delta / self._l
            lim = _DPHI_CAP / self._l
            dphi = max(-lim, min(lim, dphi))
            self._phi = _wrap180(self._phi + dphi)
            self._l += 1.0

    def _p_hat(self):
        phi = math.radians(self._phi)
        r = self._l * _UNIT
        return (self._anchor[0] + r * math.cos(phi),
                self._anchor[1] + r * math.sin(phi))

    def _goal_xy(self):
        return (self._anchor[0] + self._offset[0],
                self._anchor[1] + self._offset[1])

    # ---------------- contract ----------------

    def precondition(self, obs, ports):
        # All bookkeeping happens here, on every tick including the ones we decline:
        # the stride count has to keep advancing while the base is driving, or the
        # 1.0 m arming threshold would never be crossed.
        self._ensure()

        t = float(obs.t)
        dt = 0.0 if self._last_t is None else min(max(t - self._last_t, 0.0), _MAX_DT)
        self._last_t = t

        yaw = float(obs.pose_estimate[2])
        had_anchor = self._anchor is not None
        self._try_anchor(obs)
        if had_anchor:
            self._integrate(yaw, self._last_cmd, dt)

        # Record the base's proposal now; tick() overwrites it with what we actually
        # let through, so the integrator is always fed the executed command.
        pending = getattr(ports, "command", None)
        if pending is not None:
            self._last_cmd = (float(pending.vx), float(pending.vy))

        if self._anchor is None or obs.goal is None:
            self._bearing = None
            ports["pi_goal_bearing_valid"] = False
            return False

        gx, gy = self._goal_xy()
        px, py = self._p_hat()
        self._bearing = _wrap_pi(math.atan2(gy - py, gx - px) - yaw)
        ports["pi_goal_bearing"] = float(self._bearing)

        ready = self._travel >= _ARM_TRAVEL
        ports["pi_goal_bearing_valid"] = bool(ready)
        return ready

    def tick(self, obs, ports):
        b = self._bearing
        if b is None:
            return Status.FAILURE

        wz = max(-1.0, min(1.0, _TURN_GAIN * b))
        v_limit = _CRUISE * max(0.0, math.cos(b))

        ports.adjust(wz=wz)
        ports.cap(vx=v_limit)

        # Mirror cap semantics locally rather than re-reading the port, so the
        # integrator is fed the same number the runner will execute.
        if self._last_cmd is not None:
            base_vx, vy = self._last_cmd
            self._last_cmd = (math.copysign(min(abs(base_vx), v_limit), base_vx), vy)

        gx, gy = self._goal_xy()
        px, py = self._p_hat()
        if math.hypot(gx - px, gy - py) < _ARRIVE:
            return Status.SUCCESS
        return Status.RUNNING


PREDICTION = {
    "metric": "goal_reached",
    "baseline": "goal_seeker",
    "min_effect": 0.1,
    "cost_metric": "path_length",
}
```

The honest risk, stated plainly: on scenarios where `pose_estimate` does *not* drift, this node replaces a correct bearing with a reconstructed one that accumulates Eq. 3's signed under-rotation, and it will break episodes there. That is what the card predicts too — the claimed win is conditional on drift, and the cost metric is `path_length` precisely because near-reversals in cluttered indoor space are where Eq. 3 is weakest.
